task.description: Step 3c hard gate (REVIEWER) on ELIXIR-DEV's ISS-0480 implementation: idiom/scope/decision-record review of the two-file async:true->async:false revert plus moduledoc rewrite, per the run brief's five verification points.

result.summary:
VERDICT: PASS. This is a sound, honestly-argued, correctly-scoped two-line revert. Nothing here needed inflating and nothing here needed blocking. Findings below, in the order the brief asked for them.

===== SCOPE (brief item 2) — CONFIRMED, INDEPENDENTLY =====
`git diff main...HEAD --name-only` shows exactly: 5 handoff JSONs, orchestrator.log, registry.json, the design doc, and the two test files. `git diff main...HEAD -- test/letflow/secrets_test.exs test/letflow/webhooks_test.exs` shows only (a) the moduledoc's async-justification paragraph rewritten and (b) `use Letflow.DataCase, async: true` -> `async: false` on one line each. No other line, assertion, or fixture call in either file changed. `lib/` is completely untouched (0 files). `test/support/tenant_fixture.ex` and `test/support/data_case.ex` are not in the diff at all -- confirmed by the diff --name-only output itself, not by trusting ELIXIR-DEV's or the design's own claim of this. This is exactly what the design's §1.1/§3 said the boundary would be, and the boundary was honoured, not quietly widened. The design's explicit rejection of the fixture-source fix (§1.1: doing it right at the source is real new logic across 46 call sites and needs the same rigor ISS-0113's own two prior failed attempts required) was respected in the implementation, not reinterpreted into 'also patch the fixture a little.'

===== MODULEDOC REWRITE ACCURACY (brief item 1) — ACCURATE, EARNS ITS CLAIMS =====
Read both new moduledoc paragraphs against the actual mechanism, not just against the design doc's prose. They: (a) state the WHY, not just the new value -- name the specific DBConnection call chain (`manager.ex:169-172`'s empty-except-list check-in firing whenever the pool's mode actually changes), not merely 'reverted because of a race'; (b) correctly preserve history rather than deleting it -- both explicitly say the file's own ISS-0113 three-mechanism classification (no self-checkout, no concurrent multi-process access, no second provisioning call) was correct and is NOT retracted, distinguishing 'this file's own code was always fine' from 'a systemic fourth mechanism outside this file makes async:true unsafe for it anyway.' That is an important, easy-to-get-wrong distinction and it lands correctly; (c) correctly state the fix's sufficiency argument -- 'removes the disruptive call from the async scheduling phase entirely... which is sufficient by construction, not by continued reasoning about timing' matches ExUnit's real scheduler behaviour (verified below), not an overstated claim; (d) point forward to design §6 for the real longer-term fix rather than implying this is a permanent architecture decision. I independently verified the one load-bearing factual claim in the new prose -- that `DBConnection.Ownership.Manager.handle_call({:mode, mode}, {caller, _}, state)` checks in via `proxy_checkin_all_except(state, [], caller)` (empty except-list) specifically in the branch where the requested mode differs from `state.mode`, and no-ops via a separate clause when it matches -- by reading `deps/db_connection/lib/db_connection/ownership/manager.ex` directly myself (lines ~163-171 in this repo's vendored copy): confirmed verbatim, both clauses present and shaped exactly as the moduledoc and design describe. I also independently verified the phase-separation claim ('ExUnit runs every async: true module to completion before any async: false module starts') by reading `ex_unit/lib/ex_unit/runner.ex`'s `async_loop/4` myself: the async branch drains `running` via `wait_until_available/2` before the function's sync branch (`spawn_modules(config, [{nil, [pair]}], false, %{})`) ever executes for a `nil`-grouped (sync) module. Both claims check out against source, not merely against the handoffs' own narration of source. No overstatement found; no contradiction between the moduledoc's prose and the code found either.

===== VERIFICATION EVIDENCE ADEQUACY (brief item 3) — THE STRUCTURAL ARGUMENT CARRIES THE WEIGHT; SEEDS ARE CORROBORATION, AND THAT IS THE CORRECT WAY TO WORD IT =====
This needs to be said plainly because it changes how the claim should be phrased downstream (TEST-DESIGNER, RELEASE-VALIDATOR): the four post-fix seeds are NOT, on their own, adequate evidence for an intermittent that Step 1 itself measured at only 75% (3/4). Four clean runs after a 75%-baseline defect leaves real residual probability of a false-negative 'looks fixed' read if seeds were the only argument -- roughly a 1-in-4^4 chance of missing a defect at the ORIGINAL hit rate, better than nothing but not what should be leaned on alone, and this project's own Failure Attribution rule (core-directives.md) exists specifically to stop count-matching/small-N runs from being treated as proof. What actually closes this is the STRUCTURAL argument, and it is a materially stronger form of evidence than the seeds: §4.1's grep (independently re-run three times across three parties -- CODE-DESIGNER, CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR, ELIXIR-DEV, and I did not need a fourth run since the underlying source claim is independently confirmed) shows zero async:true files call Sandbox.mode/2 post-revert, and the manager.ex source I just read confirms that absence of a call is what removes the ONLY code path that can trigger the disruptive check-in during the async phase. A mechanism that is proven ABSENT is not probabilistic the way a seed-based stress run is -- it holds regardless of scheduling order, timing, or seed, which is exactly what 'sufficient by construction' in the moduledoc means and is the correct framing. The seeds' actual evidentiary role is narrower and still real: (a) they positively confirm the mechanism understanding is correct by reproducing the ORIGINAL defect on the same host on the very first pre-fix attempt (ELIXIR-DEV's own baseline seed-1 run failed with the exact same signature Step 1 found), which rules out 'the mechanism was already gone/misdiagnosed,' and (b) they are the only evidence available for PackUpdateMigrationTest, which has no structural argument stronger than 'shares the identical mechanism, no repro either side' (see next item). RECOMMENDATION for how the claim should be worded downstream: 'closed by construction (zero remaining Sandbox.mode/2 callers under async, verified against source), corroborated by a real same-host before/after seed comparison' -- not 'verified across 4 clean seeds,' which alone would understate the strength of the actual argument and invite exactly the count-matching mistake this project has been burned by before.

===== PACKUPDATEMIGRATIONTEST — the honestly-disclosed gap, correctly disclosed, correctly not over-claimed =====
Worth flagging on its own even though it doesn't change the verdict: unlike RowApprovalTest, there is NO empirical baseline failure for PackUpdateMigrationTest anywhere in this run's evidence (0/4 at Step 1, 0/1 at ELIXIR-DEV's own baseline attempt) -- the coverage claim rests entirely on 'same mechanism, no other explanatory code path, table-touched is irrelevant because the discard is per-connection.' That reasoning is sound (I re-checked it: the FK-insert-after-discarded-connection shape genuinely doesn't care what table is involved), but it is inference, not confirmation, and both the design (§5) and ELIXIR-DEV's handoff say so plainly rather than quietly folding it into the RowApprovalTest evidence. That is the right way to handle an unconfirmed symptom -- name the asymmetry rather than launder it into an equally-strong-sounding claim.

===== THE ISS-0423 TENSION (brief item 4) — the call to accept the revert was right; I would have made the same one =====
This needs a real opinion, not deference, so: yes, reverting was proportionate, and no, pursuing the fixture-source fix instead would have been the wrong call for THIS run. Three reasons, weighed independently of the design's own framing rather than just re-stating it: (1) Asymmetry of consequence. ISS-0423's gain here is genuinely small and already disclosed as such -- 2 of 66 async-declared files, in a suite where the two DOMINANT levers (test_parallel.sh's 2.9x, template-clone's 4.9x/provisioning) are both independent of this revert and untouched. Losing 2-of-66 files' async status is a rounding error against those. Meanwhile the cost of NOT reverting is a MAJOR, 75%-hit-rate intermittent landing in unrelated bystander tests -- in a humanless pipeline with no human to eyeball 'huh, that's probably just flaky', that is exactly the shape of failure that burns max_rework budget on whatever unlucky future requirement draws the bad seed, and directly degrades the 'green means done' property the whole pipeline depends on structurally. (2) The fixture-source alternative is not free-of-cost the way it might look on paper -- it is REAL NEW RUNTIME LOGIC across 46 call sites, and ISS-0113's own history is exactly a warning shot here: two prior real, good-faith attempts at fixing this fixture (a :manual-restore, and a restore_sandbox opt-in) were each independently verified sound, shipped for real review, and each FAILED for a distinct, previously-unconsidered mechanism only discovered after real breakage (12/125, then 26/38). A third attempt done properly needs the same source-trace-plus-multi-seed rigor those two used, against the FULL 46-site population this time (not 2), which is a materially larger, riskier undertaking than 'just fix it at the source' suggests -- and doing it under THIS issue's own severity/urgency, rather than as its own properly-scoped follow-on, is exactly the kind of under-scoped fix that produced ISS-0480 in the first place (ISS-0423's own conversion is what exposed this). (3) Reversibility. The revert is trivially undoable once a real fixture-source fix exists and is independently verified against the full call-site population -- nothing about accepting this revert now forecloses pursuing the better fix later; the design's §6 explicitly names it as the legitimate longer-term direction. Given all three, your call to accept the revert was not wrong -- it was the correctly conservative choice for a MAJOR defect against a small, already-mostly-independent throughput gain, and I would flag it as an actual mistake only if the fixture-source option had been free or already-proven-safe, which ISS-0113's own two-strikes history says it explicitly is not.

===== TEST COVERAGE / INV-1 ENFORCEMENT (brief item 5) — deferring the lint follow-on is right, WITH ONE CONDITION =====
Agree that a compile/test-time enforcement of INV-1 ('no async: true file may call Sandbox.mode/2') should be a separate, filed follow-on rather than a blocker on this fix -- this matches the project's own established pattern of splitting an enforcement/tooling lever out from a correctness fix (ISS-0427/ISS-0428 were split the same way from ISS-0423 itself, twice). Blocking this PASS on writing that lint now would be exactly the kind of scope-inflation this role is supposed to resist. The one condition: it must actually get filed as claimable work, not merely asserted in this run's prose as intended -- 'No Issue Left Local-Only' applies here specifically because this run's own task brief says 'I plan to file a lint follow-up' in first person, which is the ORCH-run-brief's own commitment, not yet a `docs/issues/ISS-NNNN.yaml` record I can point at. I did not find one on this branch (grepped docs/issues/ for INV-1/Sandbox-lint content, none exists yet). Recording this as the one actionable item from this gate: file it (title suggestion: 'No compile/test-time guard for INV-1 -- an async:true file calling Sandbox.mode/2 can silently reintroduce ISS-0480'), scoped to wiring design §4.1's grep into mix letflow.check the way the ISS-0069 substring check already works. This is a MINOR finding, not a rework trigger for THIS handoff -- ELIXIR-DEV's own diff needs no changes for it.

===== IDIOM/SUPERVISION/TYPE-SAFETY (REVIEWER's four standing questions, for completeness) =====
1. Idiomatic vs. crutch: N/A, no gen_statem/state-machine code in this diff -- this is test-file-only, ExUnit async metadata plus prose.
2. Supervision: N/A, no process/supervision code touched.
3. Type-safety gaps: N/A, no new transition logic; this is a test scheduling flag revert, no new state representable/unrepresentable by a type system either way.
4. Scope creep: none found. The diff is precisely the two lines the design specified plus the two moduledoc rewrites the design explicitly required (§1.2) -- no abstraction, macro, or generic plumbing introduced. This is the opposite of scope creep: a change that resisted the temptation to 'also fix the fixture while I'm in here.'

===== ANTI-PATTERNS CHECK =====
Checked docs/anti-patterns.md for any existing entry on Sandbox.mode/async testing/this issue family -- none exists yet (grepped for tenant_template_build, Sandbox.mode, ISS-0480, ISS-0423: no hits). This defect class (a global Sandbox.mode/2 flip discarding an unrelated bystander's connection) is new enough to this project's anti-patterns corpus that it may be worth its own entry once the lint follow-on above lands -- noting only, not filing, since anti-patterns.md entries are for the discovering/fixing run to add and this run already has one, plus the ISS-0480/ISS-0113/ISS-0423 records themselves already carry the full narrative.

===== ENVIRONMENT NOTE =====
Before starting this review I checked for orphaned erl.exe processes per the run brief's standing instruction. Found exactly one, inspected via Get-CimInstance (ProcessId 14044, ParentProcessId 12060, CommandLine referencing elixir-ls-release/launch.exs) -- confirmed this is the pre-existing ElixirLS language-server process, not a mix test worker, and left it running. I did not execute mix test/scripts/test_parallel.sh myself for this gate (my task is document/diff review against the four standing REVIEWER questions and the run brief's five verification points, not independent test execution -- that is TEST-RUNNER's/RELEASE-VALIDATOR's role downstream), so I introduced no new orphaned processes and the tenant_template/tenant_template_build_* cleanup instruction in the brief was not exercised by this step.

issues.description: The ISS-0480 design's §6 recommendation for a compile/test-time lint enforcing INV-1 ('no async: true file may call Sandbox.mode/2', wiring design §4.1's grep into mix letflow.check the way the ISS-0069 warning-substring check already works) has not yet been filed as a docs/issues/ISS-NNNN.yaml record -- grepped docs/issues/ for INV-1/Sandbox-lint content and found none. ORCH's own run brief states an intent to file this follow-up rather than block on it, which is the right call, but per 'No Issue Left Local-Only' the intent needs to actually become a filed, claimable issue (register_task) before this run closes, not remain a plan stated only in this handoff's or the run brief's prose.

Restating, for visibility, ELIXIR-DEV's own already-disclosed MINOR finding rather than a new one of my own: PackUpdateMigrationTest's FK-constraint symptom has zero empirical reproduction on either side of the fix (0/4 at Step 1, 0/1 at ELIXIR-DEV's baseline). Its coverage by this remedy rests entirely on a mechanism-level argument (identical per-connection-discard shape, table-touched is irrelevant), which I independently re-checked and find sound, but it should be worded downstream as 'covered by mechanism, not confirmed by repro' rather than folded into RowApprovalTest's stronger, repro-backed claim. Per the design's own §5 disposition (b), this is accepted as a legitimate verdict, not a gap requiring rework.

next_action: TEST-DESIGNER may proceed. Word the fix's evidentiary basis as 'closed by construction (INV-1 verified: zero async:true files call Sandbox.mode/2, confirmed against DBConnection/ExUnit source), corroborated by a real same-host before/after seed comparison' -- not as '4 clean seeds' alone, which understates the actual strength of the argument. Treat PackUpdateMigrationTest's coverage as mechanism-based, not repro-confirmed, in any test report. ORCH should ensure the INV-1 lint follow-on (MINOR finding above) is actually registered via register_task before this run closes, not left as stated-but-unfiled intent.
